welcome_lead: Today you'll meet the words and events of the Weimar Republic's struggles from 1918.

walkthroughs.body_html:
In November 1918 Kaiser Wilhelm II abdicated.

Germany became the Weimar Republic. The new government signed the armistice — earning the unfair myth of the stab-in-the-back.

The Treaty of Versailles (1919) blamed Germany, took 13% of its land, cut its army to 100,000 and demanded huge reparations.

Many Germans called it a Diktat — a forced peace. It haunted Weimar politics for years.

When Germany fell behind on reparations, France occupied the Ruhr industrial area in January 1923.

Workers struck. The government printed money. The result: hyperinflation — a loaf of bread cost billions of marks. In November, Hitler's Munich Putsch failed.

options: A peace treaty
An attempted violent takeover
A peaceful protest
A new currency

mcqs.q: Why did the French occupy the Ruhr in 1923?
options: To start a war
Germany fell behind on reparations
To free political prisoners
To stop hyperinflation

mcqs.q: How did Hitler come to power in 1933?
options: Hitler won an outright majority in the 1932 presidential election.
He was legally appointed Chancellor by President Hindenburg as part of a conservative political deal, after the Nazis became the largest party in the Reichstag.
Goebbels invented television specifically to broadcast Nazi propaganda.
Hitler seized power through a violent coup or revolution.

mcqs.q: What caused the German hyperinflation of 1923?
options: The hyperinflation was caused by the Wall Street Crash.
Reparations alone caused the hyperinflation.
Goebbels invented television specifically to broadcast Nazi propaganda.
The government printing money to pay striking workers during the French occupation of the Ruhr, on top of existing reparations and war debts.

mcqs.q: How effective was Nazi propaganda in winning popular support?
options: Nazi propaganda was so powerful that Germans believed whatever Hitler said.
Goebbels invented television specifically to broadcast Nazi propaganda.
Most effective where it reinforced existing views (anti-Versailles, fear of communism, national pride); less so when contradicting daily experience or established religious belief.
Hitler won an outright majority in the 1932 presidential election.
